messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 70

She first came to see me last autumn, though she will not call it autumn. On the islands where she grew up, there is only the wet and the dry. At fifty-seven, she is a woman who measures things: angles, load-bearing walls, the exact height of a ceiling. Her hands move when she talks, drawing invisible lines in the air. She is an architect, and she has been good at that for thirty years. But the work no longer holds her.

The story begins four years ago, during the dry season. Her daughter, Tia, was twenty-three, a marine biologist in training. Tia had been volunteering on a small research vessel, mapping coral bleaching. The boat went out one morning with a crew of five and did not come back. A sudden squall, an overloaded hull, a failure of communication—the official report was inconclusive. Tia’s body was never recovered. There was no funeral, no grave. Just a memorial plaque at the harbor, which the patient has never visited.

In the early months after the loss, she kept working. She believes now that it was a kind of denial, a way to fill the hours. She designed a community center on a neighboring island, threw herself into site visits, stayed late in the office. But the symptoms crept in like tide. She began to avoid the harbor. Then any waterfront property. Then even the sight of boats on television. She stopped going to the coast, which is difficult on an island nation where the coast is everywhere. She took inland routes, drove with her eyes fixed on the road ahead.

Intrusive memories hit her at unpredictable moments. The sound of rain on a tin roof brings back the morning of the squall. The smell of diesel makes her dizzy. Once, in a client meeting, a weather alert notification sounded on someone’s phone, and she excused herself to the restroom, where she stood for twenty minutes, pressing her palms against the cool tile, trying to steady her breath.

Her sleep fractured. She wakes at 3:00 a.m. most nights, heart pounding, convinced she has heard Tia’s voice calling from the dark. She has not had a full night’s rest in over a year. During the day, she is hypervigilant. She checks her phone obsessively for messages, even though no one would send a message from a boat that no longer exists. She cannot tolerate uncertainty. In her drawings, she now specifies every detail to the millimeter, leaving no room for ambiguity. Her colleagues call her meticulous. She knows it is something else.

Her marriage had already ended by the time Tia died, but the loss drove a wedge deeper. Her ex-husband lives on the mainland now, remarried. They do not speak. She has no other children. Her parents are gone. She has friends, but she has withdrawn from them. They mean well, but she cannot bear their pity or their silence. She stopped accepting dinner invitations. She stopped returning calls. The office has become her only social container, and even there, she keeps to herself.

The work, once a refuge, has become a battlefield. She was recently assigned to design a new boathouse for the inter-island ferry service. She took one look at the brief, felt her chest tighten, and asked for reassignment. She told her boss it was a conflict of interest. She did not explain that the project was on the same stretch of water where her daughter drowned.

There are moments when she feels almost normal. This morning, while reviewing a structural plan, she lost herself in the mathematics of a cantilever for half an hour. Then a delivery truck rumbled past the window, and for a second she saw the hull of the research vessel, tipping, and the sound of the horn—she calls it a horn, though it might have been the crew shouting—and she had to set down her pencil and breathe.

She does not know why she came to see me. She says she is not the type for therapy. She says she is an architect, and architects solve problems. But this problem cannot be solved with a blueprint. She sits in my office with her hands still, resting on her knees, and she looks at the floor. She talks about Tia in the present tense sometimes. She will say “Tia loves the water” and then stop, correct herself, and close her eyes.

Yesterday, she told me that she still leaves a blue ceramic mug on her kitchen counter, the one Tia used to drink from. She washes it every day or two. She cannot explain why. She knows it is not her daughter. But she also knows that if she puts the mug away, she will have nothing left to touch.
